extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in early childhood education (teachers, teacher-educators), and academics studying humour development
extracted.subtask_description: Frameworks and procedures for eliciting, coding, and interpreting humour production and appreciation in 60–72-month-old children (and teachers' views), using McGhee's and Martin's theories and Johnson's evaluation form. Emphasis on qualitative, phenomenological data collection (drawings, semi-structured interviews) and deductive coding.

rubrics_metrics.name: McGhee’s humour development stages
rubrics_metrics.description: McGhee defined humour development in four stages: incongruous actions towards objects (18–20 months), incongruous labelling of objects and events (20–24 months), conceptual incongruity (2–7 years), and humour with multiple meanings (7–11 years). The study treats 60–72-month-olds as in the third stage (conceptual incongruity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual incongruity: children make jokes about themselves and others, produce abstract/complex jokes, recognise 'violations of the perceptual appearances of things'. Use McGhee's stages to interpret children's production and appreciation of humour and to map age-appropriate humour types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Martin’s humour styles (adaptive vs maladaptive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Martin’s theory identifies four humour styles: two adaptive (self-enhancing; affiliative) and two maladaptive (self-defeating; aggressive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-enhancing: joking about oneself non-humiliatingly, positive outlook, supports self-worth and pro-social behaviours. Affiliative: making others laugh to facilitate relationships. Self-defeating: denigrating oneself to fit in—damages self-esteem long-term. Aggressive: humiliating others to enhance self—can harm relationships and lead to group rejection. Use Martin’s styles to categorize children’s humour use and to consider socio-emotional outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Johnson’s Evaluation Form of Humorous Factors in Children’s Books (categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: An evaluation form used to identify humorous factors in children's picture books across categories: pictorial humour types, verbal humour types, and situational humour types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pictorial examples: objects with incongruous features, physical deformities, caricature and exaggeration, masks/clowns. Verbal examples: non-language sounds, nonsense words, rhyming, erroneous labelling, puns, knock-knock jokes, irony, satire, riddles. Situational examples: pretend play with objects, tickling/body contact, potty humour, pranks, teasing, social mistakes, practical jokes. The form guided selection of the study illustration and coding of children’s drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping humour types to developmental age ranges (table-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: Table mapping age ranges (1–2 years; 2–7 years; 7+ years) to corresponding stages (McGhee / Piaget) and to likely pictorial, verbal, and situational humour types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use age-to-type mapping when evaluating whether humour in drawings/illustrations is developmentally expected (e.g., 2–7 years/Stage 3 -> conceptual incongruity, preoperational verbal forms). Apply this mapping to interpret what kinds of humour children appreciate/produce at particular ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories for coding factors included in 'funny' drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Coding categories applied to children's drawings: conceptual incongruity, physical deformity, caricature, exaggeration, costume (as listed in Table 5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associated low-level codes include: big/little people; giving human features to nonliving things; giving animal features to people; unusual physical features; unusual combinations; unusual size/number/shape/colour of body parts; hurting somebody else; unusual/inappropriate behaviours of things; exaggerated numbers; clown/nurse costumes. Use these codes to categorise elements children include to make drawings 'funny'.

rubrics_metrics.name: How children explain humour in illustrations (elicited-explanation criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Children’s appreciation of an illustration is assessed by asking them to describe what they see, whether it is funny, and why; common recognition is of incongruity (e.g., 'a giraffe is not a chair') or caricature (facial expressions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating children's explanations, prioritise whether they notice and articulate the incongruity or exaggerated features; record examples (e.g., 'The giraffe being a chair is funny' or 'the giraffe's face shows amazement'). Note variability: some children may not find the incongruity funny and may label actions as 'usual'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher-report categories for children's humour behaviours
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers classify student humour behaviour into Maladaptive Humour, Adaptive Humour, or No Humour, using specific behavioural indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maladaptive: uses physical humour that harms relationships (causes pain), leading to peer rejection. Adaptive: likes to laugh/make jokes, shares humour, uses humour alone or to include others, reflects usual things in a funny way. No Humour: child does not use humour. Use these teacher-focused categories to interpret classroom social consequences of different humour uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-collection protocol to elicit children's humour (story + drawing + interview)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure used to elicit humour: build rapport with story-reading using props, prompt children to imagine a funny event for a story character, have children draw a 'funny' picture, then conduct one-on-one interviews immediately after drawing; present a separate humorous illustration afterwards; teacher present for comfort; audio-recording and note-taking used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical points: use the more child-familiar term 'funny' rather than 'humorous'; pilot-tested story and props to reduce shyness; collect drawings from all but analyse only participants' drawings connected to the story; timing: ~30–40 minutes for story+drawing+child interview, 10–15 minutes per follow-up interview; conduct one-on-one interviews in a quiet space to avoid distractions; obtain permission for audio recording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview question categories for children (elicitation rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Semi-structured child interview categories/questions (Table 1): Views on drawing — 'What do you see in the picture?', 'Do you think that it is funny?', 'Why is it funny? What would you add to make it funnier?' etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple, concrete questions appropriate for age and language ability; adapt wording based on pilot feedback (replace 'humorous' with 'funny'); allow children to describe their drawing and the story behind it to elicit the sources of humour they used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview question categories for teachers (elicitation rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Semi-structured teacher interview topics (Table 2): demographic info ('Which university did you graduate from?', 'How many years experience?'), training ('Have you taken seminars regarding humour?'), and views on students' humour development ('How do you define the humour development of C*?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use teacher interviews to capture observational assessments of children's humour in classroom contexts, their training/knowledge about humour, and how they interpret humour-related behaviours (adaptive vs maladaptive). Pilot-test teacher questions to ensure clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding and analysis standards for qualitative humour data
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive coding approach: develop codes prior to analysis (based on Johnson's Evaluation Form, McGhee, Martin), transcribe audio, apply codes by two coders, compare and reconcile differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practices used in study: two coders (both with relevant master's-level training), most codes matched, some terms replaced by more generic terms for clarity, map codes to theoretical frameworks (McGhee's conceptual incongruity; Martin's humour styles). Present category and code tables (e.g., Tables 3–5) for transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological quality controls: pilot studies and expert review
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pilot studies with target-age children and pilot teachers plus expert review of instruments to refine interview questions, wording, and illustration selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from study: pilot with six children led to adding story-reading to reduce shyness and changing wording; experts (three professors) reviewed interview questions and illustration choices; pilot with two teachers confirmed teacher interview clarity. Use pilot feedback to adapt procedures and instruments before main data collection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical and consent requirements for research with young children
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain institutional ethics committee approval and relevant ministry/school permissions; gain parental written consent and children's verbal assent; ensure confidentiality and obtain audio-record permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study-specific: ethics approvals cited (university ethics committee and Ministry of National Education), consent letters to parents, verbal assent from children, teacher present during child interviews to provide comfort, inform participants about confidentiality before teacher interviews, and audio-record only with permission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual considerations when interpreting humour (age, development, culture, teacher bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretations of children's humour must account for age, developmental level, cultural differences, and possible teacher biases (e.g., teachers judging humour solely by social peer relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations: do not evaluate humour development only by observing social relationships; recognise cultural variation in humour perception and use (Western vs Eastern attitudes cited); consider including parents and broader samples to capture cultural/contextual variability; provide teacher training to improve observation/interpretation of children's humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional/application guideline: integrating humour into early education
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour can be used as a pedagogical tool to support learning, memory, social and emotional development, but teachers need awareness of its benefits and to adapt to age/development/culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and cautions: amusing cartoons/jokes can promote classroom learning and memory; adaptive humour supports peer acceptance, while maladaptive humour can damage relationships; teachers should model and scaffold adaptive humour via activities, environment and classroom management; lack of teacher training in humour is a limitation noted.
